newsitem.title: EGYPT: No progress on Mideast peace ahead of conference.
newsitem.headline: No progress on Mideast peace ahead of conference.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat made no progress on Middle East peace in talks before the start on Tuesday of a regional economic conference, an official said.
After a separate meeting with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, Christopher declined to answer questions on Israel's long-overdue troop redeployment from the West Bank town of Hebron.
U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns, speaking after the Christopher-Arafat meeting late on Monday, said there had been "no discernible progress" on the Middle East peace track.
Christopher met Arafat at the Egyptian Foreign Ministry as the "troika" of European Union foreign ministers prepared for what could be a difficult meeting on Tuesday with the Israelis.
Commenting on his talks with Mubarak, Christopher told reporters, without elaborating: "The president and I have discussed, as we usually do, the peace process."

Diplomats, politicians and business people are all in Cairo for the third annual Middle East and North Africa economic conference, originally called to underpin peace by integrating Israel into the regional economy.

But no last-minute breakthrough was expected in talks between Israel and the Palestinians on the Hebron pullback, regarded by the PLO as a key test of right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's professed commitment to peace.
The election of Netanyahu in May has cast the conference adrift.

The philosophy now is that Middle East countries must press on with economic reform regardless of political setbacks and that businessmen, rather than just exploiting the opportunities of peace, must add their voices to those of the peacemakers.
"It's a great rally of business leaders for peace," said Klaus Schwab, founder and president of the World Economic Forum, which is organising the event.
"It's not a conference on creating peace with Israel. It's a conference on how to achieve vast regionalisation and how to achieve also the necessary business-friendly environment.
"I think this is a very clear message...that a stable political environment, or in other words a comprehensive peace, is necessary and we expect it to come," he told reporters.
The World Economic Forum said the participants, from 92 countries, included 1,500 foreign business people, 500 Egyptian business people and between 1,500 to 2,000 government delegates.

The agenda covers big regional infrastructure projects, classic economic reforms such as privatisation and trade liberalisation, and a heavy dose of networking by the industrialists and investment bankers who are taking part.
Mubarak was opening the three-day conference on Tuesday morning after more political talks with Arafat and Christopher.

Two Israeli ministers, Natan Sharansky for commerce and industry and Dan Meridor for finance, arrived in Cairo on Monday night but the head of the delegation, Foreign Minister David Levy, was to come on Tuesday and leave later in the day.
Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring, travelling with the Italian and Dutch foreign ministers, said they would probably ask Levy to change policies crippling the Palestinian economy.

"We feel very strongly that there are opportunities in the economic sphere which the Israeli government has not in any way been helpful to. It's very important that these developments are allowed to go ahead as quickly as possible," he said.

Palestinian business people are boycotting the conference on the grounds that it does not make sense to do business with Israelis when the Israeli government is strangling the economy of the self-ruled West Bank and Gaza by closing their borders.
